summary.text: Bladder map: **M3** contracts the detrusor (void); **alpha1** closes the neck and **beta3** relaxes the detrusor (store); somatic nicotinic holds the external sphincter.
**Antimuscarinics** block M3 — dry mouth, constipation, confusion; **oxybutynin** has the highest CNS burden → older adults get **mirabegron** (beta3; may raise BP).
**Alpha1 blockers** relax the outlet in days (orthostasis, first dose, floppy iris); tamsulosin/silodosin are uroselective.
**5-ARIs** shrink the prostate over 3–6 months and **halve PSA**; often combined with an alpha1 blocker.
**PDE5 inhibitors** keep cGMP high; **any nitrate = absolute contraindication** (and caution with alpha1 blockers).

chunks.text: **Three nerve supplies, three receptor families — the physiologic foundation for every drug in this session.**
Parasympathetic M3 contracts the detrusor, sympathetic alpha-1 closes the bladder neck and beta-3 relaxes the reservoir, and somatic nicotinic control holds the external sphincter.

**Figure 9. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the parasympathetic, sympathetic, and somatic nervous systems each innervate a different structure of the lower urinary tract through a distinct receptor family —**
**the organizing map for every drug class covered this session.** Every class is anchored back to its receptor and anatomic location; Sections 5 and 6 "zoom in" on parts of this map.
Oxybutynin (blocks M3 on the detrusor), tamsulosin (blocks alpha1 at the bladder neck/prostate) and mirabegron (stimulates beta3 on the detrusor body) each target one receptor of this map.
**The parasympathetic pelvic nerve releases acetylcholine, which acts on M3 muscarinic receptors on the detrusor muscle to produce contraction — the primary driver of bladder emptying (voiding).**
M3 is the dominant muscarinic subtype in the bladder, though M2 receptors are also present in high density (smaller functional contribution normally, may increase in disease).
Chain (Figure 10): pelvic nerve releases acetylcholine → ACh binds M3 on the detrusor → Gq activates phospholipase C; calcium rises → detrusor contracts and the bladder empties.
**M3 is the dominant bladder muscarinic subtype.** **M2 is more abundant but contributes less to contraction.** **Blocking M3 underlies antimuscarinic OAB treatment.**

**The sympathetic hypogastric nerve releases norepinephrine, which acts on two different adrenergic receptor subtypes in two different locations, producing two different (and complementary) effects.**
Chain (Figure 11): sympathetic hypogastric nerve releases norepinephrine → alpha-1: outlet closed; beta-3: reservoir relaxed → continence maintained during storage.
Alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck, trigone, and proximal urethra: norepinephrine causes contraction, helping maintain continence during storage.
Beta3 receptors on the detrusor body: norepinephrine causes relaxation, allowing the bladder to fill without a premature urge to void (low pressure).
**Because M3 blockade reduces detrusor contraction, antimuscarinic drugs (Section 5) are a logical treatment for conditions of bladder overactivity.**
**Both of these receptor subtypes become specific drug targets later in this session: alpha1 blockers for BPH (Section 6), and beta3 agonists for overactive bladder (Section 5).**

Net storage effect: sympathetic tone keeps the outlet closed (alpha1) while keeping the reservoir relaxed (beta3) — parasympathetic tone is low; both arms work together for continence. During voiding, this pattern reverses.
This is applied Chapter 6: the same muscarinic family that governs other smooth muscle and glands throughout the body — the bladder is simply one more target organ.
Know which receptor does what where (alpha1 at the outlet vs. beta3 on the detrusor body) before moving on — it makes the rest of the session’s pharmacology make sense.

**Two mechanisms, one goal — calming an overactive detrusor to improve storage and reduce urgency.** Antimuscarinics block the detrusor’s muscarinic signal, while beta-3 agonists relax it.
**Figure 12. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): antimuscarinics block the M3-mediated contraction signal, while beta3 agonists enhance the norepinephrine-mediated relaxation signal —**
**two distinct mechanisms converging on the same clinical goal of improved bladder storage.** Complementary, not competing — the basis for combination therapy.
Oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin, darifenacin (antimuscarinics); mirabegron (beta3 agonist).
**Mechanism: block M3 (and, to a lesser extent, M2) muscarinic receptors on the detrusor, reducing involuntary contractions and increasing functional bladder capacity.**
Antimuscarinic agents differ mainly in receptor selectivity and anticholinergic side-effect burden rather than core mechanism.

Chain (Figure 13): drug blocks M3 receptors on the detrusor → fewer involuntary contractions, larger capacity → same blockade in brain, salivary gland and bowel → bladder relaxes, but dry mouth, constipation and confusion follow.
Oxybutynin has the highest CNS anticholinergic burden; mirabegron, a beta-3 agonist, avoids this anticholinergic burden.

**Mechanism: stimulate beta3 adrenergic receptors on the detrusor, enhancing smooth muscle relaxation during the storage/filling phase.** Mirabegron is the primary beta3 agonist in clinical use for overactive bladder.
**Key advantage: lacks the systemic anticholinergic burden of antimuscarinics, making it a preferred option in older adults or patients already on multiple anticholinergic medications.**
Mirabegron can be used alone or combined with an antimuscarinic for refractory symptoms — complementary (not redundant) mechanisms.
**Adverse effects follow directly from systemic antimuscarinic blockade: dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and — importantly — cognitive impairment and confusion, especially in older adults.**

Anticholinergic burden is cumulative across all of a patient’s medications — oxybutynin has the highest CNS anticholinergic burden of this class and is often avoided in older adults or those with dementia risk.
Mirabegron: can raise blood pressure (monitor in uncontrolled hypertension); headache or nasopharyngitis; less commonly, urinary retention.
Antimuscarinics: caution/contraindication in narrow-angle glaucoma and significant urinary retention.
Mirabegron inhibits CYP2D6. Other anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, tricyclic antidepressants) add to anticholinergic burden; cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) oppose antimuscarinics.
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) raise solifenacin levels.

Case: a 78-year-old with mild cognitive impairment and urge incontinence starts oxybutynin; three weeks later, worsening confusion and new difficulty with daily tasks. **What is the most likely explanation, and what change in therapy would you consider?**
**Oxybutynin carries a relatively high CNS anticholinergic burden, and in an older adult — especially one with pre-existing cognitive impairment — this can precipitate or worsen confusion.**

**Switching to a beta3 agonist (mirabegron), which lacks anticholinergic activity, treats the same overactive bladder symptoms without this risk.** Review other anticholinergics too (medication reconciliation).
The anticholinergic-burden-in-older-adults point is the highest-yield safety point in this section; "no anticholinergic burden" is mirabegron’s single most important advantage.
Mechanism · Antimuscarinics: Block M3 (and M2) on the detrusor · Mirabegron (beta3 agonist): Stimulate beta3 on the detrusor
Adverse effects · Antimuscarinics: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, confusion · Mirabegron (beta3 agonist): Raises BP; headache, nasopharyngitis
Older adults · Antimuscarinics: Avoid oxybutynin (highest CNS burden) · Mirabegron (beta3 agonist): Preferred — no anticholinergic burden
Cautions · Antimuscarinics: Narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention · Mirabegron (beta3 agonist): Uncontrolled hypertension; CYP2D6 inhibitor

chunks.text: Why does oxybutynin confuse an older adult? It blocks muscarinic receptors in the brain too, and anticholinergic burden adds up across every drug she takes.

**Where genitourinary pharmacology meets the cardiovascular system — alpha1 blockade, nitric oxide signaling, and a life-threatening drug interaction.** Alpha1 blockers relax the prostate; nitric oxide and cGMP drive erection.
Tamsulosin, silodosin, doxazosin, terazosin (alpha1 blockers); finasteride, dutasteride (5-ARIs); sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil (PDE5 inhibitors).
**Mechanism: block alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck, prostatic smooth muscle, and proximal urethra, relaxing outflow resistance and improving urinary flow in benign prostatic hyperplasia.**

**Figure 13. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): sympathetic norepinephrine normally contracts bladder neck and prostatic smooth muscle via alpha1 receptors, narrowing the outflow tract;**
**alpha1 blockers relax this same muscle to improve urinary flow — while the same receptor family elsewhere mediates vascular tone.**

**Mechanism: block 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT) — the same mechanism introduced in Session 1 for hirsutism and androgenetic alopecia.**
5-ARI chain (Figure 14): testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase → the enzyme makes DHT → DHT drives prostate growth → enzyme blocked, DHT falls, prostate shrinks slowly.
**Figure 15. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): non-adrenergic, noncholinergic (NANC) nerves release nitric oxide, raising cGMP and relaxing corpus cavernosum smooth muscle;**
**PDE5 normally terminates this signal by breaking down cGMP, and nitrates independently raise NO/cGMP systemically — the mechanistic basis for the absolute nitrate/PDE5-inhibitor contraindication.**

**Mechanism: block phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5), the enzyme that normally breaks down cGMP, prolonging smooth muscle relaxation in the corpus cavernosum and sustaining erectile function (Figure 15).**

Chain (Figure 16): sexual stimulation → NANC nerves release nitric oxide → guanylate cyclase makes cGMP → cGMP relaxes corpus cavernosum smooth muscle → erection. PDE5 breaks down cGMP and ends the signal.
Sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil block PDE5 and prolong the signal; an erection still needs sexual stimulation to start the pathway.
Tamsulosin, silodosin (more uroselective, less vascular effect) vs. doxazosin, terazosin (less selective, more likely to lower blood pressure systemically).
Finasteride, dutasteride: in BPH, reducing DHT shrinks prostatic tissue over time, improving urinary symptoms.

Onset: 5-ARI benefit typically takes 3–6 months, unlike the rapid onset of alpha1 blockers — the classes are frequently combined (alpha1 blocker for rapid relief, 5-ARI for long-term disease modification). Alpha1 blockers act in days; 5-ARIs take months.
PDE5 agents: sildenafil, tadalafil (longer half-life, allows more flexible dosing), vardenafil.
Finasteride is moderately effective in reducing prostate size in BPH; 1 mg/d is approved for early male pattern baldness.

**Adverse effects: orthostatic hypotension and a "first-dose effect" (pronounced hypotension with the first dose) — because alpha1 receptors also mediate vascular smooth muscle tone, not just bladder neck tone.**
Floppy iris syndrome is a recognized intraoperative complication during cataract surgery in patients on alpha1 blockers — relevant to preoperative medication reconciliation.

**Adverse effects: decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and — a key counseling point — these agents lower PSA levels by roughly half, which must be accounted for when interpreting PSA values in patients on long-term therapy.**
PDE5 common adverse effects: headache, flushing, dyspepsia, and visual disturbances (blue-tinged vision, more notable with sildenafil).
**Absolute contraindication: concurrent use with any nitrate — both raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together they can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension.**

Why absolute rather than relative: nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors independently raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together can produce profound, life-threatening hypotension — pharmacodynamic and severe regardless of dose.
**This mirrors the identical nitrate/PDE5-inhibitor warning from Unit 5's angina content, now from the opposite side of the interaction.** Riociguat is also contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors.
5-ARI pregnancy caution: finasteride/dutasteride can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus; pregnant partners should avoid handling crushed or broken tablets.
Use caution with alpha1 blockers and PDE5 inhibitors together — additive hypotension, less severe than with nitrates, still warrants spacing doses or careful monitoring.

Nitrate + PDE5 inhibitor (Figure 17): nitrate raises NO and cGMP systemically → PDE5 inhibitor stops cGMP breakdown → together, vasodilation becomes profound → severe hypotension and syncope. Never combine.
Antihypertensives: additive hypotension with alpha-1 blockers. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) raise PDE5 inhibitor levels.
Finasteride lowers DHT within 8 hours, lasting about 24 hours; dutasteride has a slow onset and a much longer half-life.
PSA falls about half on long-term 5-ARI therapy; read PSA accordingly.

**This is the exact same receptor family targeted by alpha1-blocking antihypertensives and central agents discussed in Unit 5 — the difference here is clinical intent (urinary flow vs. blood pressure), not a different drug class.**
Finasteride/dutasteride here are a deliberate callback to Session 1: same mechanism, same drugs, different clinical application.

Figure 15 applies the Chapter 6 non-adrenergic, noncholinergic neuron reading; the nitrate warning is the highest-stakes safety point in the unit — students saw it from the nitrate side in Unit 5, today from the PDE5 side.
Case: a 64-year-old with stable angina on isosorbide mononitrate asks for an ED prescription — a friend takes sildenafil "with no problems." Ask yourself: **What should the PA do, and why?**
**PDE5 inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated with any nitrate — both raise NO/cGMP signaling, and the combination can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension.**

**This prescription should not be written while the patient remains on a nitrate; the conversation should include alternative angina management or alternative ED options that do not involve this interaction, in consultation with his cardiologist.**
This case pulls a Unit 5 drug (isosorbide mononitrate) into a Unit 6 decision, making the shared NO-cGMP mechanism unmistakable.

Drug names reveal the class: **-osin** alpha1 blocker (tamsulosin, doxazosin, terazosin, silodosin; opens the outlet); **-terodine** antimuscarinic (tolterodine, fesoterodine; dampens detrusor M3 signal); **-fenacin** antimuscarinic (solifenacin, darifenacin; same class, same target).

**oxybutynin / trospium** antimuscarinic (older, higher CNS burden); **-begron** beta-3 agonist (mirabegron, vibegron; relaxes the reservoir); **-afil** PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil; keeps cGMP high).
**-steride** 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride, dutasteride; lowers DHT, shrinks prostate); **-nitrate / nitro-** nitrate (isosorbide, nitroglycerin; never with a PDE5 inhibitor).
Mechanism · Alpha1 blockers: Relax prostate/bladder-neck smooth muscle · 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors: Block testosterone → DHT; shrink the gland
Onset · Alpha1 blockers: Days · 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors: 3–6 months
Adverse effects · Alpha1 blockers: Orthostatic hypotension, first-dose effect, floppy iris · 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors: Decreased libido, ED; PSA halved
Use · Alpha1 blockers: Rapid symptom relief · 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors: Long-term disease modification — often combined

**Applying the whole genitourinary and reproductive pharmacology toolkit, across both sessions.**

**Figure 18. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the detrusor, bladder neck/prostate, and corpus cavernosum each rely on receptor families — muscarinic, adrenergic, and NO-cGMP signaling — that recur in the systemic vasculature,**
**explaining why so many genitourinary drug classes have direct cardiovascular counterparts or interactions.** Receptor families are shared with the vasculature — the unifying theme of the session.

Session 1’s gonadal hormone pharmacology (Ch. 40) and PCOS (Ch. 41 overlap) and Session 2’s autonomic bladder pharmacology (Ch. 6) are distinct but connect through shared classes — 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors appear in both sessions.
The lower urinary tract is governed by three nerve supplies and three receptor families (Figure 9): parasympathetic/M3, sympathetic/alpha1 and beta3, and somatic/nicotinic.

Antimuscarinics and beta3 agonists treat overactive bladder through complementary mechanisms — blocking contraction vs. enhancing relaxation — with anticholinergic burden the key safety differentiator in older adults.
Alpha1 blockers and 5-ARIs treat BPH through different timescales and mechanisms and are often combined; alpha1 blockade overlaps directly with Unit 5’s antihypertensive pharmacology.

The NO-cGMP pathway (Figure 15) underlies both erectile function and nitrate angina therapy (Unit 5) — therapeutic in one context, dangerous in combination in another: one of the highest-stakes safety points in the course.
Close by naming the cross-unit integration: genitourinary pharmacology shares receptor families and drug classes with cardiovascular pharmacology covered earlier in the course.
**Patient A — older adult with urge incontinence and mild cognitive impairment, needs therapy that avoids anticholinergic burden:** mirabegron (Section 5).
**Patient B — man with BPH, wants both rapid symptom relief and long-term disease modification:** combine an alpha1 blocker with a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (Section 6).
**Patient C — woman with PCOS, irregular cycles, and hirsutism, not currently trying to conceive:** combined hormonal contraception ± metformin (Session 1).

**Patient D — man with stable angina on a long-acting nitrate, requesting treatment for erectile dysfunction:** PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated; this requires a cardiology-involved conversation about alternatives.
**A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.**
**Recall Q1:** unopposed estrogen drives unchecked endometrial proliferation, raising hyperplasia and cancer risk with a uterus — a progestin is always paired unless she has had a hysterectomy.
**Recall Q2:** tamoxifen is an endometrial agonist (cancer risk) and breast antagonist; raloxifene shares breast antagonist and bone agonist effects but is essentially neutral at the endometrium.
**Recall Q3:** hyperinsulinemia stimulates ovarian theca-cell androgen production and lowers hepatic SHBG, raising free testosterone — the center of the PCOS cycle (Figure 7).

**Recall Q4:** a patient on an antimuscarinic for overactive bladder develops new confusion — switch to mirabegron, which enhances beta3-mediated detrusor relaxation without blocking muscarinic receptors.
That avoids the cumulative anticholinergic burden that can precipitate or worsen confusion in susceptible patients, particularly older adults.

**Recall Q5:** alpha1 receptors are not bladder-specific — blockade also lowers systemic vascular resistance (orthostatic hypotension, first-dose effect). **Q6:** nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors both raise NO/cGMP; combined, potentially fatal hypotension.

Integrated case: a PDE5 inhibitor should not be prescribed while this patient remains on isosorbide mononitrate — both drugs independently raise NO/cGMP signaling; the combination can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension.
This is an absolute contraindication, and any ED treatment decision must involve his cardiologist and consideration of whether his anginal nitrate therapy can be modified first.

Even without the nitrate, tamsulosin and a PDE5 inhibitor both lower blood pressure (alpha1 blockade and NO-cGMP potentiation) — additive orthostatic hypotension warrants spacing doses or close monitoring.
His wife’s new vaginal bleeding on tamoxifen should not be dismissed — tamoxifen’s endometrial agonism raises hyperplasia/cancer risk; she needs prompt gynecologic evaluation.

U6-R11.question: What three receptor families govern the storage versus voiding phases of bladder function, and where is each one located?
U6-R11.answer: Parasympathetic/M3 receptors on the detrusor drive contraction (voiding); sympathetic/alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck/urethra drive contraction (continence); sympathetic/beta3 receptors on the detrusor body drive relaxation (storage).

U6-R12.question: What is the mechanism of antimuscarinic agents in overactive bladder, and which agent in this class carries the highest CNS anticholinergic burden?
U6-R12.answer: Antimuscarinics block M3 (and M2) receptors on the detrusor to reduce involuntary contractions; oxybutynin carries the highest CNS anticholinergic burden of the class.

U6-R13.question: How does mirabegron's mechanism differ from that of the antimuscarinics, and which patient population benefits most from that difference?
U6-R13.answer: Mirabegron stimulates beta3 receptors to enhance detrusor relaxation without any anticholinergic activity, making it preferred in older adults or those already on multiple anticholinergic drugs.

U6-R14.question: What distinguishes uroselective alpha1 blockers (tamsulosin, silodosin) from nonselective ones (doxazosin, terazosin), and what adverse effect do all of them share regardless of selectivity?
U6-R14.answer: Tamsulosin/silodosin are uroselective with less vascular effect, while doxazosin/terazosin are nonselective and more likely to lower systemic blood pressure; all alpha1 blockers share the risk of orthostatic hypotension and a first-dose effect.

U6-R15.question: What is the expected onset of symptomatic benefit with 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors in BPH, and what commonly ordered lab value must be reinterpreted in a patient on long-term therapy?
U6-R15.answer: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors take 3–6 months for symptomatic benefit in BPH and lower PSA by roughly half, a value that must be adjusted for when interpreting PSA in patients on long-term therapy.

U6-R16.question: Why is concurrent use of a PDE5 inhibitor with any nitrate an absolute contraindication rather than a relative one?
U6-R16.answer: Nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors both independently raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together can produce profound, life-threatening hypotension — an absolute rather than relative contraindication because the interaction is pharmacodynamic and severe regardless of dose or timing.

U6-S.question:
A 67-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia (nocturia, weak urinary stream) is started on tamsulosin. His history includes stable angina managed with isosorbide mononitrate and long-standing erectile dysfunction, for which he now asks about adding "the pill my friend takes for ED." His wife, who was recently started on tamoxifen for ER-positive breast cancer, mentions to him in passing that she's had some unexpected spotting, and he asks whether he should be worried about her.
Is it appropriate to prescribe a PDE5 inhibitor for this patient given his current medication regimen, and what is the pharmacologic reasoning?
Setting the nitrate issue aside entirely, is there still a reason to be cautious about combining a PDE5 inhibitor with his tamsulosin, and why?
What should be said about his wife's new bleeding on tamoxifen, and is it something to dismiss as incidental?
U6-S.answer: A PDE5 inhibitor should not be prescribed while this patient remains on isosorbide mononitrate — both drugs independently raise NO/cGMP signaling, and the combination can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension; this is an absolute contraindication, and any ED treatment decision must involve his cardiologist and consideration of whether his anginal nitrate therapy can be modified first. Independent of the nitrate issue, tamsulosin and PDE5 inhibitors both lower blood pressure through overlapping vasodilatory mechanisms (alpha1 blockade and NO-cGMP potentiation, respectively), so even without the nitrate, combining them carries an additive orthostatic hypotension risk that warrants spacing doses or close monitoring. His wife's new vaginal bleeding on tamoxifen should not be dismissed: tamoxifen acts as an estrogen receptor agonist at the endometrium even while antagonizing the receptor in breast tissue, and this tissue-selective agonism raises the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer — new abnormal bleeding on tamoxifen warrants prompt gynecologic evaluation.

tree.name: Part 1 · Autonomic Control of the Lower Urinary Tract

children.name: Class
facts: **Three nerve supplies, three receptor families — the physiologic foundation for every drug in this session.**
Parasympathetic M3 contracts the detrusor, sympathetic alpha-1 closes the bladder neck and beta-3 relaxes the reservoir, and somatic nicotinic control holds the external sphincter.

**Figure 9. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the parasympathetic, sympathetic, and somatic nervous systems each innervate a different structure of the lower urinary tract through a distinct receptor family —**
**the organizing map for every drug class covered this session.** Every class is anchored back to its receptor and anatomic location; Sections 5 and 6 "zoom in" on parts of this map.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Oxybutynin (blocks M3 on the detrusor), tamsulosin (blocks alpha1 at the bladder neck/prostate) and mirabegron (stimulates beta3 on the detrusor body) each target one receptor of this map.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **The parasympathetic pelvic nerve releases acetylcholine, which acts on M3 muscarinic receptors on the detrusor muscle to produce contraction — the primary driver of bladder emptying (voiding).**
M3 is the dominant muscarinic subtype in the bladder, though M2 receptors are also present in high density (smaller functional contribution normally, may increase in disease).
Chain (Figure 10): pelvic nerve releases acetylcholine → ACh binds M3 on the detrusor → Gq activates phospholipase C; calcium rises → detrusor contracts and the bladder empties.
**M3 is the dominant bladder muscarinic subtype.** **M2 is more abundant but contributes less to contraction.** **Blocking M3 underlies antimuscarinic OAB treatment.**

**The sympathetic hypogastric nerve releases norepinephrine, which acts on two different adrenergic receptor subtypes in two different locations, producing two different (and complementary) effects.**
Chain (Figure 11): sympathetic hypogastric nerve releases norepinephrine → alpha-1: outlet closed; beta-3: reservoir relaxed → continence maintained during storage.
Alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck, trigone, and proximal urethra: norepinephrine causes contraction, helping maintain continence during storage.
Beta3 receptors on the detrusor body: norepinephrine causes relaxation, allowing the bladder to fill without a premature urge to void (low pressure).

children.name: Indications
facts: **Because M3 blockade reduces detrusor contraction, antimuscarinic drugs (Section 5) are a logical treatment for conditions of bladder overactivity.**
**Both of these receptor subtypes become specific drug targets later in this session: alpha1 blockers for BPH (Section 6), and beta3 agonists for overactive bladder (Section 5).**

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Net storage effect: sympathetic tone keeps the outlet closed (alpha1) while keeping the reservoir relaxed (beta3) — parasympathetic tone is low; both arms work together for continence. During voiding, this pattern reverses.
This is applied Chapter 6: the same muscarinic family that governs other smooth muscle and glands throughout the body — the bladder is simply one more target organ.
Know which receptor does what where (alpha1 at the outlet vs. beta3 on the detrusor body) before moving on — it makes the rest of the session’s pharmacology make sense.

children.name: Class
facts: **Two mechanisms, one goal — calming an overactive detrusor to improve storage and reduce urgency.** Antimuscarinics block the detrusor’s muscarinic signal, while beta-3 agonists relax it.
**Figure 12. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): antimuscarinics block the M3-mediated contraction signal, while beta3 agonists enhance the norepinephrine-mediated relaxation signal —**
**two distinct mechanisms converging on the same clinical goal of improved bladder storage.** Complementary, not competing — the basis for combination therapy.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin, darifenacin (antimuscarinics); mirabegron (beta3 agonist).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: block M3 (and, to a lesser extent, M2) muscarinic receptors on the detrusor, reducing involuntary contractions and increasing functional bladder capacity.**
Antimuscarinic agents differ mainly in receptor selectivity and anticholinergic side-effect burden rather than core mechanism.

Chain (Figure 13): drug blocks M3 receptors on the detrusor → fewer involuntary contractions, larger capacity → same blockade in brain, salivary gland and bowel → bladder relaxes, but dry mouth, constipation and confusion follow.
Oxybutynin has the highest CNS anticholinergic burden; mirabegron, a beta-3 agonist, avoids this anticholinergic burden.

**Mechanism: stimulate beta3 adrenergic receptors on the detrusor, enhancing smooth muscle relaxation during the storage/filling phase.** Mirabegron is the primary beta3 agonist in clinical use for overactive bladder.

children.name: Indications
facts: **Key advantage: lacks the systemic anticholinergic burden of antimuscarinics, making it a preferred option in older adults or patients already on multiple anticholinergic medications.**
Mirabegron can be used alone or combined with an antimuscarinic for refractory symptoms — complementary (not redundant) mechanisms.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Adverse effects follow directly from systemic antimuscarinic blockade: dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and — importantly — cognitive impairment and confusion, especially in older adults.**

Anticholinergic burden is cumulative across all of a patient’s medications — oxybutynin has the highest CNS anticholinergic burden of this class and is often avoided in older adults or those with dementia risk.
Mirabegron: can raise blood pressure (monitor in uncontrolled hypertension); headache or nasopharyngitis; less commonly, urinary retention.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Antimuscarinics: caution/contraindication in narrow-angle glaucoma and significant urinary retention.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Mirabegron inhibits CYP2D6. Other anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, tricyclic antidepressants) add to anticholinergic burden; cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) oppose antimuscarinics.
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) raise solifenacin levels.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Case: a 78-year-old with mild cognitive impairment and urge incontinence starts oxybutynin; three weeks later, worsening confusion and new difficulty with daily tasks. **What is the most likely explanation, and what change in therapy would you consider?**
**Oxybutynin carries a relatively high CNS anticholinergic burden, and in an older adult — especially one with pre-existing cognitive impairment — this can precipitate or worsen confusion.**

**Switching to a beta3 agonist (mirabegron), which lacks anticholinergic activity, treats the same overactive bladder symptoms without this risk.** Review other anticholinergics too (medication reconciliation).
The anticholinergic-burden-in-older-adults point is the highest-yield safety point in this section; "no anticholinergic burden" is mirabegron’s single most important advantage.

tree.name: Part 3 · BPH, Erectile Dysfunction & PDE5 Inhibitors

children.name: Class
facts: **Where genitourinary pharmacology meets the cardiovascular system — alpha1 blockade, nitric oxide signaling, and a life-threatening drug interaction.** Alpha1 blockers relax the prostate; nitric oxide and cGMP drive erection.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Tamsulosin, silodosin, doxazosin, terazosin (alpha1 blockers); finasteride, dutasteride (5-ARIs); sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil (PDE5 inhibitors).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: block alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck, prostatic smooth muscle, and proximal urethra, relaxing outflow resistance and improving urinary flow in benign prostatic hyperplasia.**

**Figure 13. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): sympathetic norepinephrine normally contracts bladder neck and prostatic smooth muscle via alpha1 receptors, narrowing the outflow tract;**
**alpha1 blockers relax this same muscle to improve urinary flow — while the same receptor family elsewhere mediates vascular tone.**

**Mechanism: block 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT) — the same mechanism introduced in Session 1 for hirsutism and androgenetic alopecia.**
5-ARI chain (Figure 14): testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase → the enzyme makes DHT → DHT drives prostate growth → enzyme blocked, DHT falls, prostate shrinks slowly.
**Figure 15. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): non-adrenergic, noncholinergic (NANC) nerves release nitric oxide, raising cGMP and relaxing corpus cavernosum smooth muscle;**
**PDE5 normally terminates this signal by breaking down cGMP, and nitrates independently raise NO/cGMP systemically — the mechanistic basis for the absolute nitrate/PDE5-inhibitor contraindication.**

**Mechanism: block phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5), the enzyme that normally breaks down cGMP, prolonging smooth muscle relaxation in the corpus cavernosum and sustaining erectile function (Figure 15).**

Chain (Figure 16): sexual stimulation → NANC nerves release nitric oxide → guanylate cyclase makes cGMP → cGMP relaxes corpus cavernosum smooth muscle → erection. PDE5 breaks down cGMP and ends the signal.
Sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil block PDE5 and prolong the signal; an erection still needs sexual stimulation to start the pathway.

children.name: Indications
facts: Tamsulosin, silodosin (more uroselective, less vascular effect) vs. doxazosin, terazosin (less selective, more likely to lower blood pressure systemically).
Finasteride, dutasteride: in BPH, reducing DHT shrinks prostatic tissue over time, improving urinary symptoms.

Onset: 5-ARI benefit typically takes 3–6 months, unlike the rapid onset of alpha1 blockers — the classes are frequently combined (alpha1 blocker for rapid relief, 5-ARI for long-term disease modification). Alpha1 blockers act in days; 5-ARIs take months.
PDE5 agents: sildenafil, tadalafil (longer half-life, allows more flexible dosing), vardenafil.
Finasteride is moderately effective in reducing prostate size in BPH; 1 mg/d is approved for early male pattern baldness.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Adverse effects: orthostatic hypotension and a "first-dose effect" (pronounced hypotension with the first dose) — because alpha1 receptors also mediate vascular smooth muscle tone, not just bladder neck tone.**
Floppy iris syndrome is a recognized intraoperative complication during cataract surgery in patients on alpha1 blockers — relevant to preoperative medication reconciliation.

**Adverse effects: decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and — a key counseling point — these agents lower PSA levels by roughly half, which must be accounted for when interpreting PSA values in patients on long-term therapy.**
PDE5 common adverse effects: headache, flushing, dyspepsia, and visual disturbances (blue-tinged vision, more notable with sildenafil).

children.name: Contraindications
facts: **Absolute contraindication: concurrent use with any nitrate — both raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together they can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension.**

Why absolute rather than relative: nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors independently raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together can produce profound, life-threatening hypotension — pharmacodynamic and severe regardless of dose.
**This mirrors the identical nitrate/PDE5-inhibitor warning from Unit 5's angina content, now from the opposite side of the interaction.** Riociguat is also contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors.
5-ARI pregnancy caution: finasteride/dutasteride can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus; pregnant partners should avoid handling crushed or broken tablets.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Use caution with alpha1 blockers and PDE5 inhibitors together — additive hypotension, less severe than with nitrates, still warrants spacing doses or careful monitoring.

Nitrate + PDE5 inhibitor (Figure 17): nitrate raises NO and cGMP systemically → PDE5 inhibitor stops cGMP breakdown → together, vasodilation becomes profound → severe hypotension and syncope. Never combine.
Antihypertensives: additive hypotension with alpha-1 blockers. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) raise PDE5 inhibitor levels.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Finasteride lowers DHT within 8 hours, lasting about 24 hours; dutasteride has a slow onset and a much longer half-life.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: PSA falls about half on long-term 5-ARI therapy; read PSA accordingly.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: **This is the exact same receptor family targeted by alpha1-blocking antihypertensives and central agents discussed in Unit 5 — the difference here is clinical intent (urinary flow vs. blood pressure), not a different drug class.**
Finasteride/dutasteride here are a deliberate callback to Session 1: same mechanism, same drugs, different clinical application.

Figure 15 applies the Chapter 6 non-adrenergic, noncholinergic neuron reading; the nitrate warning is the highest-stakes safety point in the unit — students saw it from the nitrate side in Unit 5, today from the PDE5 side.
Case: a 64-year-old with stable angina on isosorbide mononitrate asks for an ED prescription — a friend takes sildenafil "with no problems." Ask yourself: **What should the PA do, and why?**
**PDE5 inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated with any nitrate — both raise NO/cGMP signaling, and the combination can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension.**

**This prescription should not be written while the patient remains on a nitrate; the conversation should include alternative angina management or alternative ED options that do not involve this interaction, in consultation with his cardiologist.**
This case pulls a Unit 5 drug (isosorbide mononitrate) into a Unit 6 decision, making the shared NO-cGMP mechanism unmistakable.

Drug names reveal the class: **-osin** alpha1 blocker (tamsulosin, doxazosin, terazosin, silodosin; opens the outlet); **-terodine** antimuscarinic (tolterodine, fesoterodine; dampens detrusor M3 signal); **-fenacin** antimuscarinic (solifenacin, darifenacin; same class, same target).

**oxybutynin / trospium** antimuscarinic (older, higher CNS burden); **-begron** beta-3 agonist (mirabegron, vibegron; relaxes the reservoir); **-afil** PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil; keeps cGMP high).
**-steride** 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride, dutasteride; lowers DHT, shrinks prostate); **-nitrate / nitro-** nitrate (isosorbide, nitroglycerin; never with a PDE5 inhibitor).

tree.name: Part 4 · Putting It All Together: GU Toolkit

children.name: Key definitions
facts: **Applying the whole genitourinary and reproductive pharmacology toolkit, across both sessions.**

**Figure 18. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the detrusor, bladder neck/prostate, and corpus cavernosum each rely on receptor families — muscarinic, adrenergic, and NO-cGMP signaling — that recur in the systemic vasculature,**
**explaining why so many genitourinary drug classes have direct cardiovascular counterparts or interactions.** Receptor families are shared with the vasculature — the unifying theme of the session.

children.name: How it works
facts: Session 1’s gonadal hormone pharmacology (Ch. 40) and PCOS (Ch. 41 overlap) and Session 2’s autonomic bladder pharmacology (Ch. 6) are distinct but connect through shared classes — 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors appear in both sessions.
The lower urinary tract is governed by three nerve supplies and three receptor families (Figure 9): parasympathetic/M3, sympathetic/alpha1 and beta3, and somatic/nicotinic.

Antimuscarinics and beta3 agonists treat overactive bladder through complementary mechanisms — blocking contraction vs. enhancing relaxation — with anticholinergic burden the key safety differentiator in older adults.
Alpha1 blockers and 5-ARIs treat BPH through different timescales and mechanisms and are often combined; alpha1 blockade overlaps directly with Unit 5’s antihypertensive pharmacology.

The NO-cGMP pathway (Figure 15) underlies both erectile function and nitrate angina therapy (Unit 5) — therapeutic in one context, dangerous in combination in another: one of the highest-stakes safety points in the course.
Close by naming the cross-unit integration: genitourinary pharmacology shares receptor families and drug classes with cardiovascular pharmacology covered earlier in the course.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: **Patient A — older adult with urge incontinence and mild cognitive impairment, needs therapy that avoids anticholinergic burden:** mirabegron (Section 5).
**Patient B — man with BPH, wants both rapid symptom relief and long-term disease modification:** combine an alpha1 blocker with a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (Section 6).
**Patient C — woman with PCOS, irregular cycles, and hirsutism, not currently trying to conceive:** combined hormonal contraception ± metformin (Session 1).

**Patient D — man with stable angina on a long-acting nitrate, requesting treatment for erectile dysfunction:** PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated; this requires a cardiology-involved conversation about alternatives.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: **A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.**
**Recall Q1:** unopposed estrogen drives unchecked endometrial proliferation, raising hyperplasia and cancer risk with a uterus — a progestin is always paired unless she has had a hysterectomy.
**Recall Q2:** tamoxifen is an endometrial agonist (cancer risk) and breast antagonist; raloxifene shares breast antagonist and bone agonist effects but is essentially neutral at the endometrium.
**Recall Q3:** hyperinsulinemia stimulates ovarian theca-cell androgen production and lowers hepatic SHBG, raising free testosterone — the center of the PCOS cycle (Figure 7).

**Recall Q4:** a patient on an antimuscarinic for overactive bladder develops new confusion — switch to mirabegron, which enhances beta3-mediated detrusor relaxation without blocking muscarinic receptors.
That avoids the cumulative anticholinergic burden that can precipitate or worsen confusion in susceptible patients, particularly older adults.

**Recall Q5:** alpha1 receptors are not bladder-specific — blockade also lowers systemic vascular resistance (orthostatic hypotension, first-dose effect). **Q6:** nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors both raise NO/cGMP; combined, potentially fatal hypotension.

children.name: Exam traps
facts: Integrated case: a PDE5 inhibitor should not be prescribed while this patient remains on isosorbide mononitrate — both drugs independently raise NO/cGMP signaling; the combination can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension.
This is an absolute contraindication, and any ED treatment decision must involve his cardiologist and consideration of whether his anginal nitrate therapy can be modified first.

Even without the nitrate, tamsulosin and a PDE5 inhibitor both lower blood pressure (alpha1 blockade and NO-cGMP potentiation) — additive orthostatic hypotension warrants spacing doses or close monitoring.
His wife’s new vaginal bleeding on tamoxifen should not be dismissed — tamoxifen’s endometrial agonism raises hyperplasia/cancer risk; she needs prompt gynecologic evaluation.

Match each drug or drug class to its mechanism or site of action — tamoxifen: breast antagonist, bone/endometrium agonist; raloxifene — endometrium neutral; finasteride/dutasteride — 5-alpha-reductase inhibition; oxybutynin — M3 (and M2) antagonism on the detrusor.

Match: mirabegron — beta3 agonism on the detrusor; tamsulosin — uroselective alpha1 antagonism; sildenafil/tadalafil — PDE5 inhibition prolonging cGMP; metformin (PCOS) — insulin sensitization, indirectly lowering ovarian androgens.
